newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Gloom falls as gold gurus eye dull prospects.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gloom falls as gold gurus eye dull prospects.

text.p: The final session of the two-day Financial Times Gold Conference ended on Tuesday in almost funereal silence as experts predicted lower prices and a lack of investment interest in the metal.
"This is the most negative sentiment I have ever seen at these events," said Stewart Murray, chief executive of the gold industry's leading market research group Gold Fields Minerals Services.
"Usually people get a bit if a lift but not this time," he added as around 400 gold buffs filed out of the conference room.
There were countless reasons according to gold industry executives and market players but it boiled down to there being no good reason for investing in gold long term to make money.
And that meant there was very little likelihood of the gold price lifting from stagnant and depressed levels around $340 per ounce where it has been slumped most of the year.
Ironically physical demand for gold was at high levels during the first four months of the year and was only predictably dropping off as the northern hemisphere summer lull took over.
But according to mining analysts at the conference, a $340 gold price was perilously close to the production cost of many mines in key production areas like South Africa and Australia.
One observer pinpointed a year-end price of $305 having forecast a level around $350 three months ago.
At a dinner for Merrill Lynch clients attending the conference the company's London-based metal market analyst Ted Arnold went even further, suggesting gold prices might fall to $250.
"One problem is the perception that any rally will be aborted by producers hedging metal to take advantage of the higher price," said Murray.
Also hanging over the market was the spectre of the central banks eyeing their 35,000 tonnes of gold reserves with a view to selling at least part of that stockpile.

Holding gold rather than interes-earning assets like bonds costs the central banks collectively about $15 billion a year in lost interest, according Union Bank of Switzerland bullion analyst Andy Smith.
He called for the national banks to clear the air by announcing a co-ordinated sales policy.

During the final session's panel discussion Martin Senn, managing director precious metals at Credit Suisse First Boston said gold as a percentage of Swiss private banks' investor portfolios was close to zero from 10-15 percent a few years ago.
"Demand is subdued from European investors. There is pressure from uncertainties over official sector (central bank) sales," Senn said.
But he added that selling from private investors was unlikely as they had worked their gold holdings down over the past five years.

Minoru Ikeda, general manager derivative products in Mitsui and Co's commodity trading and risk management division said gold had been a bad asset for Japanese investors over the past five-10 years when they would have lost 57 percent of their investments.
Help from the heavily-moneyed U.S. hedge funds was unlikely, according to Fred Bogart, manager precious metals at Republic Bank of New York.
"All they want to do is make money and they don't care how they do it. Gold may be a small part of their portfolio but they would just as soon trade any commodity that is moving," he said.

A report from academics working for the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank (central bank) released on Friday suggested the world's central banks' gold reserves gave them little benefit and they should be liquidated -- sold to investors.
The study estimated that the impact would reduce the gold price by $41 given that gold miners would stop selling the product.
"This was purely a discussion document. It is nothing to do with Fed policy," said one central banking source.
"The market is tired," said market analyst Rhona O'Connell at London-based stockbroker T. Hoare and Co.

She noted International Monetary Fund plans last year to sell some gold by auction to raise funds for poor countries, a Swiss plan to revalue its gold reserves and a similar and even more controversial scheme in Germany.
"With all that going on I can think of many reasons why the price should go down. Working out why it should go up is much more difficult," said an analyst at a major London bullion house.
